target: Ni ellir newid y gorffennol.
english: The past cannot be changed.
tip: ‘ellir’ is the impersonal can-form and needs no subject: ‘ni ellir newid’ = one cannot change.

target: Mae hi'n byw ym Mangor ers blynyddoedd.
english: She's lived in Bangor for years.
tip: With ‘ers’ (for), Welsh keeps the present tense to mean has been: ‘mae hi'n byw ... ers’ = she has lived for.

target: Mae hi'n gweithio mor galed â'i chydweithwyr.
english: She works as hard as her colleagues.
tip: For as ... as, use ‘mor ... â’; ‘mor’ soft-mutates the adjective: ‘caled’ becomes ‘galed’. ‘mor galed â’ = as hard as.

target: Dysgodd hi siarad Cymraeg yn yr ysgol.
english: She learned to speak Welsh at school.
tip: Welsh needs no word for 'to' between two verbs: ‘dysgodd hi siarad’ = she learned to speak. ‘siarad’ stays plain.

target: Mae tair ystafell wely yn ein tŷ ni.
english: There are three bedrooms in our house.
tip: ‘tair’ is the feminine three, used with feminine nouns: ‘tair ystafell’ = three rooms. Masculine takes ‘tri’.

target: Gofynnodd y plentyn pam mae'r awyr yn las.
english: The child asked why the sky is blue.
tip: Reported questions keep statement order, with ‘mae’ straight after ‘pam’: ‘pam mae'r awyr yn las’ = why the sky is blue.

target: Hoffwn i ddysgu sut i baentio tirluniau Cymreig.
english: I'd like to learn how to paint Welsh landscapes.
tip: ‘hoffwn i’ = I would like, and the next verb soft-mutates: ‘dysgu’ becomes ‘ddysgu’. ‘hoffwn i ddysgu’ = I'd like to learn.

target: Mae pen tost gen i, oes paracetamol gyda chi?
english: I've got a headache, do you have paracetamol?
tip: Welsh has no verb for have: ‘mae pen tost gen i’ = there is a sore head with me, so I have a headache. ‘gen i’ = with me.

target: Mae fy nghar i wedi torri, dw i angen help.
english: My car has broken down, I need help.
tip: After ‘fy’ (my), ‘c’ nasal-mutates to ‘ngh’: ‘car’ becomes ‘nghar’. ‘fy nghar i’ = my car.

target: Coginiodd Nerys ginio blasus i'r teulu ddoe.
english: Nerys cooked a tasty lunch for the family yesterday.
tip: A past-tense verb's object soft-mutates: ‘cinio’ becomes ‘ginio’. ‘coginiodd Nerys ginio’ = Nerys cooked lunch.

target: Beth yw enw'r ci?
english: What's the dog's name?
tip: Welsh links two nouns for 'of' with no separate word: ‘enw'r ci’ means the dog's name, literally name the-dog.

target: Pam na ddest ti?
english: Why didn't you come? (informal)
tip: ‘na’ turns a why-question negative and soft-mutates the verb: ‘dest’ becomes ‘ddest’ in ‘pam na ddest ti’ (why didn't you come).

target: Pryd mae dy ben-blwydd di?
english: When is your birthday?
tip: ‘dy’ (your) soft-mutates the next word and often echoes with ‘di’: ‘pen’ becomes ‘ben’ in ‘dy ben-blwydd di’ (your birthday).

target: Dywed wrtha i beth ddigwyddodd.
english: Tell me what happened.
tip: After ‘beth’ (what) a verb soft-mutates: ‘digwyddodd’ becomes ‘ddigwyddodd’. ‘beth ddigwyddodd’ = what happened.

target: Does dim bara ar ôl.
english: There's no bread left.
tip: ‘does dim’ means there is no and sits right before the noun: ‘does dim bara’ (there's no bread). It denies existence, not an action.

target: Dw i eisiau'r un glas.
english: I want the blue one.
tip: ‘eisiau’ is the exception to the ‘yn’ rule: no ‘n’ comes before it, as in ‘dw i eisiau'r un glas’ (I want the blue one).

target: Un ferch a dau fachgen.
english: One girl and two boys.
tip: ‘un’ before a feminine noun causes soft mutation: ‘merch’ becomes ‘ferch’ in ‘un ferch’ (one girl).

target: Does dim tocynnau ar ôl.
english: There are no tickets left.
tip: ‘ar ôl’ placed after a noun means left or remaining: ‘dim tocynnau ar ôl’ (no tickets left).

target: Ble alla i barcio'r car?
english: Where can I park the car?
tip: ‘alla i’ (can I) soft-mutates the verb that follows: ‘parcio’ becomes ‘barcio’ in ‘ble alla i barcio'r car’.

target: Beth ydy ystyr y gair hwn?
english: What does this word mean?
tip: 'this' and 'that' follow the noun in Welsh: ‘y gair hwn’ means this word, literally the word this.

target: Ydy hi'n mynd i fwrw glaw?
english: Is it going to rain?
tip: ‘mynd i’ plus a verb makes the future and soft-mutates it: ‘bwrw’ becomes ‘fwrw’ in ‘mynd i fwrw glaw’ (going to rain).

target: Mae hi'n gallu siarad tair iaith.
english: She can speak three languages.
tip: Use ‘tair’, not ‘tri’, for three before a feminine noun: ‘tair iaith’ (three languages).

target: Cymerwch yr ail dro ar y dde.
english: Take the second turn on the right.
tip: The ‘-wch’ ending marks a formal or plural command: ‘cymerwch’ (take). The informal single-person form drops it: ‘cymer’.

target: Dyw hi ddim yn gwybod am y newid.
english: She doesn't know about the change.
tip: ‘ddim’ does the negating and follows the subject: ‘dyw hi ddim yn gwybod’ (she doesn't know), verb then subject then ‘ddim’.

target: Disgwylir i'r tywydd wella.
english: The weather is expected to improve.
tip: The ‘-ir’ ending makes a verb impersonal, with no named doer: ‘disgwylir’ means is expected in ‘disgwylir i'r tywydd wella’.

target: Paentiodd e'r gegin y penwythnos diwethaf.
english: He painted the kitchen last weekend.
tip: Feminine nouns soft-mutate after ‘y’ or ‘'r’ (the): ‘cegin’ becomes ‘gegin’. ‘paentiodd e'r gegin’ = he painted the kitchen.

target: Prynodd hi dair torth o fara.
english: She bought three loaves of bread.
tip: ‘torth’ is feminine, so three is ‘tair’ not ‘tri’, here mutated to ‘dair’: ‘dair torth’ = three loaves.

target: Mae siarad dwy iaith yn fantais.
english: Speaking two languages is an advantage.
tip: The linking ‘yn’ soft-mutates the word after it, so ‘mantais’ turns into ‘fantais’ in ‘yn fantais’.

target: Mae e'n gryfach nag y mae'n edrych.
english: He is stronger than he looks.
tip: The ‘-ach’ ending makes an adjective comparative, more: ‘gryfach’ means stronger in ‘mae e'n gryfach’.

target: Dylai fe ymddiheuro am beth ddwedodd e.
english: He should apologise for what he said.
tip: ‘dylai’ means should or ought to: ‘dylai fe ymddiheuro’ = he should apologise. It has no plain past form.
